analysis.one_liner: Stops medical bills from showing up on credit reports for a year and wipes paid-off ones off.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on February 3, 2021, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal credit reporting law so that a medical bill could not appear on your credit report until it is at least a year old, giving people time to pay it, settle it, dispute it, or work out insurance coverage first. Any medical debt that is fully paid or settled would have to be wiped off a credit report within 45 days. Debt collectors would also have to send written notice before reporting a medical bill to the credit bureaus, and could not report it during that first year.
analysis.who_benefits: People who get sick or hurt and end up with medical bills — a group that cuts across every income level. Millions of Americans have medical debt on their credit reports, and a lowered credit score can raise the cost of a car loan, a mortgage, an apartment, or even a job offer. Under this bill, a one-time hospital bill would no longer immediately drag down a credit score, and paying off medical debt would actually repair the score instead of the record lingering for years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills on their credit

how_it_helps.text: Bars credit bureaus from including any medical debt less than one year old on a consumer's credit report.
Requires credit reports to drop fully paid or settled medical debt within 45 days of payment.

Requires anyone about to report medical debt to send the consumer written notice first, including the exact date the one-year waiting period ends, and to warn the consumer that paying or settling the debt during that year means it never gets reported at all — giving them time to pursue insurance coverage or financial assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors, hospitals, and other medical providers that use credit reporting as a collection lever would lose some of that leverage during the first year of a bill, and would face a new notice requirement. Credit bureaus would have to build new filters to screen out medical debt by age and payment status. Some lenders argue they would extend credit with less complete information, though the bill's stated purpose is more accurate credit information.

drawbacks.text: Lenders lose access to information about recent unpaid medical bills for a year, which they argue is a real signal of financial distress; screening applicants becomes less complete in the short run.
The one-year shield is temporary, not an exemption: an unpaid medical bill would still land on a credit report after a year, so the underlying burden of medical debt remains untouched.
Hospitals and collectors could still sue and garnish over medical debt during the waiting period; the bill only delays what shows up at the credit bureaus, not the debt itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and broad: medical debt is unusually common, often not the consumer's fault (surprise bills, insurance disputes), and its damage to credit scores outlasts the debt itself. The costs are real but modest — a temporary information gap for lenders and compliance changes for collectors and bureaus — and the bill is deliberately narrow rather than forgiving debt or capping charges. The main honest criticism is that it treats a symptom: after a year, the debt is still there and still reportable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on February 3, 2021 with three Democratic cosponsors: Menendez, Blumenthal, and Van Hollen.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors and the credit reporting bureaus kept the ability to put medical bills on credit reports immediately, and hospitals and collection agencies kept credit reporting as a collection tool. Nobody's medical debt was relieved.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the record shows no floor debate or vote, so partisan positions beyond sponsorship are unknown.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and medical providers that report debts
industries.note: They would lose the ability to threaten a person's credit score during the first year of a medical bill and would face a new notice duty. That reporting threat is a common lever for pressuring people to pay quickly.
Bureaus would have to exclude young medical debts and purge paid ones within 45 days, changing their data products. Some elements of medical-debt reporting are a source of their data completeness.

industries.industry: Mortgage, auto, and other consumer lenders
industries.note: They would not see medical bills under a year old, trading some information for a borrower pool whose scores better reflect true ability to repay. The bill frames this as improving credit-market information.
